reconcile.connective: GILL argues Jesus never enjoins literal hatred — contrary to God's own law — but only that family not be loved more than Christ.

discrepancy.connective: Gerd Theissen argues Luke's family-renunciation ethic reflects the real practice of the wandering-charismatic Jesus movement — a stance the later household code genuinely reverses.

skeptic.name: Gerd Theissen
skeptic.attribution: Gerd Theissen, Sociology of Early Palestinian Christianity, trans. John Bowden (Philadelphia: Fortress, 1978), pp. 8-16

excerpts.excerpt_text: not that proper hatred of any, or all of these, is enjoined by Christ; for this would be contrary to the laws of God, to the first principles of nature, to all humanity, to the light of nature, to reason and divine revelation: but that these are not to be preferred to Christ, or loved more than he …
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly denies that Jesus commands literal hatred, grounding the denial in 'the laws of God' — the same divine-law footing Ephesians' household commands stand on — and reduces 'hate' to not-preferring-above-Christ, which is compatible with honoring parents and loving one's wife.

pd_work.resource: John Haley, An Examination of the Alleged Discrepancies of the Bible (1874)
pd_work.author: John Haley
pd_work.note: Haley devotes a page-286 parallel-column heading, 'Kindred, how regarded: Hated. — Loved.', setting Luke 14:26 directly against Ephesians 5:25, 33, and resolves it via the Hebrew-idiom sense of 'hate' as 'to love less,' quoting Moses Stuart and Henry Alford.

link.note: Live apologetic treatment of the same comparative-hatred reading (cross-referencing Mark 7:9-13 and 1 Timothy 5:8 rather than Ephesians, but directly on-topic to Luke 14:26 itself).
